catalog_quote: 2.3. Prosodemes There are two distinctive prosodemes (DP) characterized by a contrast of the syllabic tones. In isolated words, DP I consists of a stressed high tone, whereas DP II consists of a stressed falling tone. The distinctive prosodemes are marked in this paper by strokes over the vowels of the bearing syllables, DP I as á and DP II as â. Again, minimal pairs of lexemes based on this contrast alone are rare. However, the prosodic features have also a grammatical function, for instance in marking relative clauses, subjunctives or nouns followed by a qualifier. new_statements.rule_in_words: No source states where word stress falls. The only first-hand phonological description (Möhlig 1986) treats Ilwana prosody as a two-way tonal contrast (high vs falling) realized on stressed 'bearing' syllables whose position is marked per word, with few lexical minimal pairs and clear grammatical functions (relatives, subjunctives, noun + qualifier); Möhlig et al. 1986[1984] call the tone/accent system distinctive with 'very complicated rules' and note a 'strong accent' conditioning open vowel allophones. Nurse 1994 says outright that he does not know the Ilwana accent system; Nurse & Hinnebusch 1993 say 'of Elwana we know next to nothing' prosodically (2-4 tones reported; Philippson: tones seem to work like Pokomo's, where penult prominence is length only and 'rather less audible'); Nurse 2000 (Philippson's analysis of Nurse's recordings) concludes tentatively: lexical tone in nominal/adjectival stems, verb roots not tonally distinctive, tone important in conjugation (person/TAM). Net: a poorly described restricted-tone / tonal-accent system; a Sabaki-type penult prominence is plausible by analogy with Pokomo but is nowhere asserted for Ilwana.
new_statements.secondary_stress: Nothing said in any source seen.
new_statements.exceptions: Möhlig 1986: lexical minimal pairs for the DP I/DP II contrast are rare; prosody marks relative clauses, subjunctives and noun + qualifier. Nurse 2000 (Philippson): 1st/2nd vs 3rd person subject forms differ by tone in the -ie past (cf. Nurse 2008 App.2 u-cek-ie 'you laughed' vs u-cék-ie 'he laughed'). Möhlig et al. 1986[1984]: open allophones [e, o] of /ɪ, ʊ/ appear under strong accent.
new_statements.domain_note: Möhlig 1986 explicitly describes 'isolated words' (citation forms); grammatical uses are phrase-level (noun followed by qualifier, relative clauses). Vowel length is contrastive (Möhlig 1986 sec. 2.2), so penult length in Nurse 2008 transcriptions (u-fi:le, tw-a:kw-i:ta, gy-a:kw-á:bana) cannot be read as demarcative lengthening without the source saying so.
new_statements.identity_note: All sources refer to the same single language, ilwa1237: 'Elwana' in Nurse 1985 and Nurse & Hinnebusch 1993, 'Ilwana' in Möhlig 1986 and Nurse 1994/2000, 'Ki-ilwana' in Nurse 2008, autonym Kiwilwana, exonym Malakote/Malankote (ISO mlk, Guthrie E701). No dialects are distinguished. Möhlig's statements rest on his own Atlas Dialectal du Kenya fieldwork (1970s, villages Masa/Chewele area on the middle Tana); Nurse 2000's tone paragraph rests on Nurse's recordings analysed instrumentally by G. Philippson (Lyon). Not to be confused with 'Ilwana' F22G, a Nyamwezi/Sukuma-area variety indexed separately in The Bantu Languages (2019).

sources.note: Transcribed verb forms only, with tone marks, vowel length and a downstep: tu-cek-ie 'we laughed', u-cek-ie 'you laughed' vs u-cék-ie 'he laughed', n-é:-cek-íé 'I laughed', ni-muku-lI!m-é:ni 'I am cultivating', n-a:ko-sóm-á 'I will read', gy-a:kw-á:ban-a 'it will fall', bUzi u-f-i:le 'the goat is dead'. Shows grammatical tone (2sg vs 3sg by tone alone); no prose on stress.
